doc.title: Ray Conniff interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998

title: Keeping cuts around 2:15 for radio airplay
summary: Radio programmers favored shorter songs, so Conniff timed arrangements carefully, with exceptions such as 'On the Street Where You Live'.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: I’ve noticed that at that time you had a timeframe that you had to work in, or that you chose to work in, for each song, that as I look at these titles, the longest cut I see is like three minutes and fifteen seconds. Was that mostly for a radio consideration or was it just for the listeners’ attention span?

Well there were two things that went into that. The radio was a very big part of it, airplay. If you had a song that was 3:15 and someone else had a song that was 2:15, and the guy’s making up his show, he would pick the 2:15 unless he really wanted to play, you know, because he wanted to get more commercials in. And we were all kind of keeping our cuts down as much as we could, because we got a better chance of airplay on the cuts if they were around 2:15 — 2:20 was ideal. To go under it you were getting, the buyer wasn’t getting enough music, and you didn’t really have a chance to get a good idea in the arrangements. The other thing was that on the album sides, long cuts — well let’s see — we were putting out twelve songs to an album originally, six on a side. And they
eventually cut that to five on a side because of the royalties and the payments for the songs you know. Let’s see you asked about the timing.

So if you write your arrangement then, you had to actually figure out what’s the tempo of this song, and kind of time like how many choruses can I do, should I go to the bridge here sooner than I was going to. You had to keep in mind the time as you put the structure of the song together.
